lead: JavaScript is the language a browser runs inside a web page. It lets a page react: read a value, compare it, choose a branch, repeat a step. A program is just a list of statements, run top to bottom. Variables hold values, operators combine values, and control statements decide which statements run. The same ideas power form checks, UPI payment buttons, and live cricket score widgets. This chapter covers the base syntax that every later JavaScript topic in this unit assumes.
prereq: You need: an HTML page from Unit 2 to hold the script, and the browser console from Unit 1 to read output.

sections.h3: A script in a page, output, and data types

blocks.text: Put JavaScript inside an HTML page in one of two ways. An inline script sits between <script> and </script>. An external file is loaded with <script src='app.js'></script>. Put the tag just before </body>, or add defer to an external script. defer downloads the file now but runs it after the HTML is parsed, in file order.
To see a value, use console.log(value); it prints to the browser console. alert(value) shows a popup. Use the console while debugging and alert only for a real user message.

JavaScript has these data types: number (72, 3.14), string ('C'), boolean (true, false), null (a deliberate empty value), undefined (a variable with no value yet), object (a collection; arrays are objects), symbol (a unique key), and bigint (a whole number written with n, like 10n). typeof value returns a string naming the type. Two quirks: typeof null is 'object', and typeof function is 'function'.

Automatic type coercion means JavaScript converts a value when an operator needs another type. '5' * 2 gives 10, because * forces numbers. '5' + 2 gives '52', because + joins strings when either side is a string. Arrays and objects are covered in 3.2.

Declare a variable with var, let or const. var is function scoped: a var inside a block leaks to the whole function, and it can be redeclared. let is block scoped: it exists only inside the nearest { }, cannot be redeclared in that block, and can be reassigned. const is block scoped and must be initialised; the name cannot be reassigned. Prefer const; use let only when the value changes. Avoid var in new code.
Arithmetic operators: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide, % remainder, ** power. Assignment operators store: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=. Comparison: >, <, >=, <=, ==, ===, !=, !==.
== converts types and compares value; === compares value and type with no conversion. So '5' == 5 is true, but '5' === 5 is false. Use === and !== unless you have a reason.

blocks.where: condition is any expression; valueIfTrue runs when condition is truthy; valueIfFalse runs when it is falsy.

blocks.text: Logical: && and, || or, ! not. Nullish: a ?? b returns b only when a is null or undefined. Difference: 0 || 5 gives 5, but 0 ?? 5 gives 0, because || treats 0 as false. Precedence: ** before * / %, then + -, then comparisons, then &&, then ||, then ?:, then assignment. Use parentheses to be clear.

if (condition) statement runs the statement when condition is truthy. Falsy values are false, 0, '', null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy. Add else for the other path. Chain tests with else if: JavaScript checks from top to bottom and runs only the first true branch. The figure traces marks = 72 through an else-if ladder.
switch (expression) compares expression with each case value using ===. break exits the switch. Without break, control falls through into the next case. default runs when no case matches.

Loops repeat. for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) runs init once, tests before each pass, and updates after each pass. while (condition) tests first. do { ... } while (condition) runs the body once, then tests. for (const x of array) walks values in order. break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next update or test. Changing the page itself is 3.4.

figure.caption: The ladder tests 72 against 90, then 75, then 60. Only the third test is true, so it prints C and every other branch is skipped.

spec.title: else-if ladder for marks = 72
spec.aria: A top-down else-if ladder for marks 72: the tests 72 ≥ 90 and 72 ≥ 75 are false, the test 72 ≥ 60 is true, so the program prints C and skips the other print steps.

examples.question: A student scores 72 out of 100. Write a JavaScript else-if ladder, and an equivalent switch, that prints A for 90 or above, B for 75 or above, C for 60 or above, and D otherwise. Then write a for loop that prints the sum 1+2+3+4+5. State every output.
steps: Set marks = 72. First test: 72 >= 90 is false.
Third test: 72 >= 60 is true, so the ladder prints C and skips the rest.
The switch(true) form tests the same cases with ===. Case 72 >= 90 is false, case 72 >= 75 is false, case 72 >= 60 is true, so it prints C and break exits.
For the loop, sum starts at 0. i = 1 gives sum = 1; i = 2 gives 3; i = 3 gives 6; i = 4 gives 10; i = 5 gives 15.
Next i = 6, test 6 <= 5 is false, loop ends, and console.log(sum) prints 15.
examples.answer: The ladder prints C, the switch prints C, and the loop prints 15.

traps: Using == where === is meant: '5' == 5 is true but '5' === 5 is false.
A var declared inside a block leaks out of that block; let and const do not.
A switch case with no break falls through into the next case, so two messages may print.
A do-while body runs once even when the condition is false on the first test.
typeof null returns 'object', not 'null'; that is a long-standing JavaScript quirk.

quiz.q: Name three primitive data types in JavaScript and give one typeof result.
quiz.a: Number, string and boolean are primitive. typeof 72 gives 'number'.

quiz.q: Why is const preferred over let when a value does not change?
quiz.a: const is block scoped and cannot be reassigned, so the reader knows the name keeps one value. let allows reassignment, which is needed only for changing values.

quiz.q: What does this print? let x = 5; x += '5'; console.log(x);
quiz.a: x starts as number 5. The += with a string converts to string joining, so x becomes '55'. Output: 55.

quiz.q: Write the output of: let s = 0; for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { s += i; } console.log(s);
quiz.a: s becomes 1, then 3, then 6, then 10. Output: 10.

quiz.q: A switch has case 80: console.log('B'); with no break, then default: console.log('D');. marks is 80. What prints and why?
quiz.a: It prints B then D. The matching case runs, and without break control falls through into default.
'5' == 5 is true because == converts the string to a number. '5' === 5 is false because === also checks type, and string is not number.

quiz.q: State one difference between while and do-while.
quiz.a: while tests before the first pass, so the body may run zero times. do-while runs the body once before the first test, so it runs at least once.

quiz.q: What does this print? let n = 7; console.log(n % 2 === 0 ? 'even' : 'odd');
quiz.a: 7 % 2 is 1, and 1 === 0 is false, so the ternary picks 'odd'. Output: odd.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real projects add strict mode, modules and TypeScript so type mistakes are caught before the browser runs the file. Linters such as ESLint can ban == and warn about unused variables. Build tools then bundle many small JavaScript files into one file for the browser. Search next for JavaScript strict mode, ESLint eqeqeq, and TypeScript type narrowing.
